guide.title: Russian Hill, San Francisco: Lombard Street's crooked block, three National Register districts and the hilltop parks
guide.intro: Russian Hill is a residential hill on the north side of San Francisco, climbed by the Powell-Hyde cable car and crossed by Polk, Hyde, Green and Broadway. Almost everything a visitor comes for is outdoors. The crooked block of Lombard Street, eight hairpin turns of red brick between Hyde and Leavenworth, is here. So are three districts on the National Register of Historic Places, none of which contains the others; a pedestrian lane a novelist named as the model for a fictional one; an art school that closed in 2022 with a Diego Rivera fresco inside it; two old fire houses and a Moorish Revival cinema now used as a gym; a garden by Thomas Church open 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.; hilltop tennis courts laid over a covered reservoir; and a road tunnel driven under the hill in 1952. The shops and restaurants sit on Polk Street and on the Hyde Street cable car blocks.

sections.heading: Three districts on one hill
sections.body:
The federal register carries three separate districts here, and their names all begin with Russian Hill. They do not nest inside one another and they are not the same kind of place.

The Russian Hill-Vallejo Street Crest District, National Register reference number 87002289, was listed on 22 January 1988. It covers roughly 1020-1032 Broadway, 1-49 Florence Street, 1728-1742 Jones Street, 1-7 Russian Hill Place, 1629-1715 Taylor Street and 1000-1085 Vallejo Street: the crest of the hill, whose streets are engineered against grades of 16, 23 and 40 percent with retaining walls, ramps and walkways. The enclave escaped the 1906 fire, which is why houses of the 1850s still stand in it.

The Russian Hill-Paris Block Architectural District, reference number 87002288, was listed on 7 January 1988 and is one block of Green Street, roughly 1017-1067, on 1.5 acres: eleven dwellings in eleven architectural styles, all set back behind front yards. The houses on the north side back onto Macondray Lane.

The Russian Hill-Macondray Lane District, reference number 87002286, was listed the same day and covers 1.6 acres around the lane, with twelve contributing buildings and one contributing site. Four houses inside it survived the 1906 earthquake and fire.

What is not here is a city historic district. San Francisco's Article 10 register of historic districts includes none of the three, so a Russian Hill address may carry an individual city landmark number without standing inside a city district.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
The Powell-Hyde cable car runs the length of the hill on Hyde Street and stops at Hyde and Lombard Streets, at the top of the crooked block. The Muni stop page prints it as Hyde St & Lombard St, number 15078, with service from 7 a.m. to 11 p.m. daily. The cable car climbs; the hill it climbs is steep everywhere, and the Vallejo Street crest reaches grades of 40 percent, so steer by addresses and cross streets rather than by lines on a map.

Broadway passes beneath the hill instead of over it, through the Robert C. Levy Tunnel, 1,616 feet of two bores with two lanes each. The west portal is just east of the Hyde Street overpass and the east portal just east of the Mason Street overpass.

Useful addresses for orientation: 800 Chestnut Street for the art institute campus, 1088 Green Street for Engine Company No. 31, 1067 Green Street for the Feusier Octagon House, 801 Bay Street for Francisco Park, 2366 Leavenworth Street for Fay Park, 1200 Greenwich Street for the Alice Marble Courts, and 2320-2336 Polk Street for the Alhambra. Macondray Lane runs between Leavenworth and Taylor Streets, parallel to Union and Green, and a set of wooden steps descends from the lane down to Taylor Street.

sections.heading: Parks, and what time they open
sections.body:
Eight of the neighbourhood's parks and playgrounds are Recreation and Parks property, and most of them keep the department's standard hours of 5 a.m. to midnight. One does not, and it is the one to plan a day around.

Fay Park, at Leavenworth and Chestnut Streets, opens 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. It is a garden of about a third of an acre on three terraces, designed by Thomas Church, with stone balustrades, boxwood hedges, two latticed wooden gazebos and an overlook onto San Francisco Bay. The house beside it is not open to the public.

Francisco Park, at 801 Bay Street, opened in April 2022 on the site of the 1859 Francisco Reservoir. It runs 5 a.m. to midnight across 4.5 acres bordered by Francisco, Larkin, Bay and Hyde streets, with a community garden, a children's playground and nature exploration area, a fenced dog run, accessible pathways and a rainwater catchment system. Ina Coolbrith Park at Vallejo and Taylor Streets and Michelangelo Playground at Greenwich and Jones Streets both keep their restrooms on shorter hours than the parks themselves: 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. at Ina Coolbrith, and 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. in spring and summer at Michelangelo, closing at 5.30 p.m. in autumn and winter.

The hilltop courts are the other habit of the neighbourhood. The Alice Marble Courts at Greenwich and Hyde, laid over the covered Lombard Reservoir, hold four tennis courts, a basketball court and a practice wall; Helen Wills Playground at Broadway and Larkin holds tennis and basketball courts, paved playfields and a clubhouse.

faq.question: Where is the crooked block of Lombard Street, and can you drive it?
faq.answer: It is the block of Lombard Street between Hyde and Leavenworth Streets. Eight hairpin turns of red brick descend about 600 feet of roadway across 412.5 feet in a straight line, working around a hillside grade of 27 percent. Traffic is one way, downhill only, and a sign at the top of the block recommends 5 miles per hour. The block normally carries around 250 vehicles an hour, and average daily traffic on it was 2,630 vehicles in 2013. The Powell-Hyde cable car stops at Hyde and Lombard Streets, at the top of the block.

faq.question: Was Macondray Lane really the model for Barbary Lane?
faq.answer: Armistead Maupin said so himself. In the 2017 documentary The Untold Tales of Armistead Maupin he confirmed Macondray Lane as the model for Barbary Lane in Tales of the City. The lane runs two blocks between Leavenworth and Taylor Streets, parallel to Union and Green, with a view north to Alcatraz Island and San Francisco Bay, and a set of wooden steps descending to Taylor Street. It is a contributing site of the Russian Hill-Macondray Lane District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1988, reference number 87002286.

faq.question: Can you go inside the San Francisco Art Institute at 800 Chestnut Street?
faq.answer: The school closed in July 2022 and filed for Chapter 7 liquidation on 26 April 2023; in late February 2024 a nonprofit backed by Laurene Powell Jobs bought the campus for about 30 million dollars. The Diego Rivera Gallery, which housed Rivera's 1931 fresco The Making of a Fresco Showing the Building of a City, closed when the school did. No source states opening hours for the campus. The buildings can be seen from Chestnut Street.

faq.question: Are the historic houses open to visitors?
faq.answer: No. The Feusier Octagon House at 1067 Green Street, the Atkinson-Escher House at 1032 Broadway and the House of the Flag at 1652-1656 Taylor Street are private residences with no public access. Each carries a city designation: San Francisco Landmark No. 36, No. 97 and No. 46 respectively. No source states opening hours for Engine Company No. 31 at 1088 Green Street. The Church for the Fellowship of All Peoples at 2041 Larkin Street holds a Convocation each October that is open to the public.

faq.question: Which streets carry the shops and restaurants?
faq.answer: Two: Polk Street and the Hyde Street cable car blocks. Polk Street carries Cheese Plus at 2001 Polk Street, at Pacific Avenue, and the Russian Hill Bookstore at 2162 Polk Street; the Alhambra of 1926 stands at 2320-2336 Polk Street and now houses a Crunch Fitness gym behind its restored marquee. The Hyde Street cable car blocks carry Frascati at 1901 Hyde Street and Za Pizza at 1919 Hyde Street, both at Green Street.

photos.title: The crooked block of Lombard Street, looking east
photos.description: Two of the hairpin turns on the one-way block of Lombard Street between Hyde and Leavenworth Streets, paved in red brick and divided by planted beds, with Telegraph Hill and the San Francisco-Oakland Bay Bridge beyond.
photos.author: Supercarwaar

places.name: Lombard Street's crooked block
places.summary: The one-way block of Lombard Street between Hyde and Leavenworth Streets, laid out in eight hairpin turns and paved in red brick. Traffic runs downhill only. A sign at the top of the block recommends 5 miles per hour. The roadway is about 600 feet long and covers 412.5 feet in a straight line. The Powell-Hyde cable car stops at Hyde and Lombard Streets, at the top of the block.
places.history: The switchbacks were built in 1922, to a design first suggested by the property owner Carl Henry as a way of working around the hillside's 27 percent grade. The block normally carries around 250 vehicles an hour, and average daily traffic on it was 2,630 vehicles in 2013.

places.name: Macondray Lane
places.summary: A pedestrian lane running two blocks east and west between Leavenworth and Taylor Streets, parallel to Union and Green. A set of wooden steps descends from the lane to Taylor Street, and the view north takes in Alcatraz Island and San Francisco Bay.
places.history: The lane is a contributing site of the Russian Hill-Macondray Lane District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 7 January 1988, reference number 87002286, and carried by the California Office of Historic Preservation as N1542. The district covers roughly 900-982 Green Street, 1918-1960 Jones Street, 15-84 Macondray Lane and 1801-1809 Taylor Street: 1.6 acres, with twelve contributing buildings and one contributing site. Four houses in the district survived the 1906 earthquake and fire, and 982 Green Street was built in 1878. In the 2017 documentary The Untold Tales of Armistead Maupin, Maupin confirmed the lane as the model for Barbary Lane in Tales of the City.

places.name: Russian Hill-Vallejo Street Crest District
places.summary: The residential crest of the hill, listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 22 January 1988, reference number 87002289, and carried by the California Office of Historic Preservation as N1549. It covers roughly 1020-1032 Broadway, 1-49 Florence Street, 1728-1742 Jones Street, 1-7 Russian Hill Place, 1629-1715 Taylor Street and 1000-1085 Vallejo Street. The listing included two contributing sites and five contributing structures. The streets are open to walk; the houses are private.
places.history: The enclave escaped the 1906 fire. Its street treatment is Beaux-Arts, with retaining walls, ramps and walkways engineered against grades of 16 percent, 23 percent and 40 percent. Work by Willis Polk, Charles F. Whittlesey, Julia Morgan, Albert Farr and Charles W. McCall stands inside the boundary, together with buildings by the amateur architect Joseph Worcester. Residents named in the nomination include Katherine Atkinson, Maynard Dixon, Sara Bard Field, Dorothea Lange, Rose Wilder Lane, Horatio P. Livermore, Willis Polk, Mary Curtis Richardson and Dora Norton Williams.

places.name: Russian Hill-Paris Block Architectural District
places.summary: One block of Green Street, roughly 1017-1067, covering 1.5 acres: eleven single and multiple dwellings in eleven architectural styles, every one of them set back behind a front yard. The houses on the north side of the street back onto Macondray Lane. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 7 January 1988, reference number 87002288, and the California Office of Historic Preservation carries it as N1543.
places.history: The name Paris Block appears in print no earlier than 1964. The nomination suggests it refers to the Bos Apartments at 1050 Green Street, built in 1891 to a design by the Beaux-Arts-trained architect Lewis P. Hobart. The Feusier Octagon House at 1067 Green Street stands inside the boundary.

places.name: San Francisco Art Institute
places.summary: A Spanish Colonial Revival campus by Bakewell & Brown, which the school moved into in 1926. A later addition by Paffard Keatinge-Clay brought 22,500 square feet of studio space, a theater and lecture hall, galleries, a cafe, and an outdoor amphitheatre formed by the stepped roof of the lecture hall. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 85, designated in 1977, and listed on the National Register of Historic Places under reference number 15000950. No source states opening hours for the campus.
places.history: The school began in 1871 as the San Francisco Art Association, became the California School of Fine Arts in 1916 and took the name San Francisco Art Institute in 1961. Diego Rivera painted The Making of a Fresco Showing the Building of a City on the campus in 1931; the fresco itself is San Francisco Landmark No. 294, designated in 2021, which is an unusual thing for a city to designate. In January 2021 the trustees proposed selling the fresco to the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art and dropped the plan after objections. The school closed in July 2022, taking the Diego Rivera Gallery that housed the work with it, and filed for Chapter 7 liquidation on 26 April 2023. In late February 2024 a nonprofit backed by Laurene Powell Jobs bought the campus, fresco included, for about 30 million dollars.

places.name: Engine Company No. 31 Fire House
places.summary: A fire house of 1908 on Green Street between Hyde and Leavenworth. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 220, designated in 1998, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1988, reference number 87002290. No source states its opening hours.
places.history: The building dates from 1908. Two registers carry it under two names at the same address: the city's Article 10 register as Engine Company Number 31 Fire House, and the federal register as Engine House No. 31.

places.name: Alhambra Theater
places.summary: A Moorish Revival cinema at 2320-2336 Polk Street, with two turrets outside and a kaleidoscope domed ceiling inside. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 217, designated in 1996. The building now houses a Crunch Fitness gym; the original marquee has been restored and films are still shown on the screen.
places.history: It opened on 5 November 1926 with 1,625 seats, at a cost of 500,000 dollars, to a design by Miller & Pflueger. Timothy L. Pflueger also designed the Castro Theatre and the Paramount in Oakland. The auditorium was twinned in 1976 and returned to a single screen in 1988, and it closed as a cinema on 22 February 1998.

places.name: Feusier Octagon House
places.summary: An eight-sided house on Green Street, later given a third storey, a mansard roof and a cupola. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 36, designated in 1970, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1974, reference number 74000554. One of three octagon houses in San Francisco. It is a private residence with no public access.
places.history: George Kenny built the house in about 1857 and 1858; it was sold in 1870 to Louis Feusier, whose family name it now carries. The Article 10 register spells it Feusier Octagon House/Kenny Residence. It contributes to the Russian Hill-Paris Block Architectural District, National Register reference number 87002288.

places.name: Atkinson House
places.summary: A house of 1853 on the Vallejo Street crest, San Francisco Landmark No. 97, designated in 1977. The city register names it the Atkinson-Escher House. It is a private residence and cannot be visited.
places.history: It was built in 1853 by the architect William H. Ranlett with the contractor Charles Homer and the mason Joseph H. Atkinson, who between them put up three houses on what is now the Vallejo Street crest in 1853 and 1854. The house came through the 1906 earthquake, and it contributes to the Russian Hill-Vallejo Street Crest District, National Register reference number 87002289.

places.name: House of the Flag
places.summary: A house at 1652-1656 Taylor Street. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 46, designated in 1972, and the city register carries it under two names, House Of The Flag and Old Sheppard-Dakin Hs. It is a private residence with no public access.
places.history: No register that carries the building states a build date or an architect for it.

places.name: Filbert Street Cottages
places.summary: Cottages on Filbert Street, San Francisco Landmark No. 232, designated in 2003. They are private property, seen from the pavement.
places.history: The city's Article 10 record carries the property under three names: the Filbert Street Cottages, the Bush Cottages, and the School of Basic Design and Color. No source states an architect or a build date for them.

places.name: Church for the Fellowship of All Peoples
places.summary: A church on Larkin Street with an off-white stucco front, three arched inset doors at street level and a leaning bell tower. The congregation describes itself as intercultural, interracial, interfaith and interdenominational, and holds a Convocation each October, open to the public, at which it presents the Howard Thurman Award. The city register spells the name Church for the Fellowship of All People: it is San Francisco Landmark No. 309, designated in 2023.
places.history: Wikipedia records that the congregation was founded in 1944 by Howard Thurman and Alfred Fisk, and that Thurman left a tenured post at Howard University to help the Fellowship of Reconciliation establish it.

places.name: Engine Co. No. 8, Truck Co. No. 4
places.summary: A fire house at 1648 Pacific Avenue. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 188, designated in 1988, and the city register carries it as Engine Co. #8, Truck Co. #4.
places.history: No register that carries the building states a build date or an architect for it.

places.name: Broadway Tunnel (Robert C. Levy Tunnel)
places.summary: The road tunnel that carries Broadway under Russian Hill, officially the Robert C. Levy Tunnel. It is 1,616 feet long, in two bores of two lanes each. The west portal is just east of the Hyde Street overpass and the east portal just east of the Mason Street overpass.
places.history: In 1863 the California State Assembly granted Abner Doble, I. T. Pennel, Joseph M. Wood and I. W. Cudworth the right to tunnel through Russian Hill, on the line of Broadway street, from Mason street to Hyde or Larkin street. Nothing came of it. Bion J. Arnold revived the idea in a report to the city in March 1913. City voters approved a 5 million dollar bond for the work in 1948, and the tunnel opened on 21 December 1952.

places.name: Francisco Park
places.summary: A 4.5-acre park bordered by Francisco, Larkin, Bay and Hyde streets, opened in April 2022 and open daily from 5 a.m. to midnight. Recreation and Parks lists a community garden, a children's playground and nature exploration area, a fenced dog run, accessible pathways, native plants and trees, and a sustainable rainwater catchment system. From the terraces you can see the Golden Gate Bridge, Ghirardelli Square, Alcatraz and the Palace of Fine Arts.
places.history: The park occupies the site of the Francisco Reservoir, constructed in 1859 and shut down in 1940 after the Lombard Reservoir opened a block away; the ground was fenced off from then until the park was built. Recreation and Parks bought the land for 9.9 million dollars, and the Francisco Park Conservancy raised 27.5 million dollars to build the park.

places.name: Fay Park
places.summary: A garden of about a third of an acre at Leavenworth and Chestnut Streets, open 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Three terraces climb the hillside for half a city block, linked by stairs and ramps, with stone balustrades and retaining walls, ornamental planting beds and boxwood hedges, two latticed wooden gazebos, and an overlook at the top with a view of San Francisco Bay.
places.history: The Fay family built the first house on the site in 1869 and the present house in 1912. Brigadier General Paul Berrigan commissioned the landscape architect Thomas Church to design the garden in 1957. The garden and the house came to the city by bequest from his wife, Mary Fay Berrigan; the city accepted the property on the general's death in 1998 and opened the garden to the public in 2006. The house is not open to the public.

places.name: Ina Coolbrith Park
places.summary: A steep 0.87-acre park at Vallejo and Taylor Streets, terraced into the hillside. It is open from 5 a.m. to midnight, and the restroom from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.
places.history: The park is named for the writer and librarian Ina Coolbrith, who is named in the National Register nomination for the Russian Hill-Macondray Lane District, reference number 87002286.

places.name: Alice Marble Courts
places.summary: 0.84 acres of hard courts at Greenwich and Hyde Streets, open 5 a.m. to midnight: four accessible tennis courts, a full-court outdoor basketball court and a practice wall. Recreation and Parks describes them as sitting atop Russian Hill and George Sterling Park.
places.history: The courts are laid over the Lombard Reservoir, water-utility land the city records at 1200 Greenwich Street. They are named for the tennis player Alice Marble, who won eighteen Grand Slam titles between 1936 and 1940.

places.name: Michelangelo Playground
places.summary: A 0.48-acre playground at Greenwich and Jones Streets, with a basketball court, a community garden, a picnic area, a grassy area and restrooms. The park is open 5 a.m. to midnight; the restrooms open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. in spring and summer and 8 a.m. to 5.30 p.m. in autumn and winter.
places.history: No source states a history for the playground.

places.name: Helen Wills Playground
places.summary: 0.92 acres at Broadway and Larkin Streets, with tennis courts, basketball courts, a children's play area, paved playfields and a clubhouse. The park is open 5 a.m. to midnight.
places.history: The playground is named for the tennis player Helen Wills.

places.name: Hyde & Vallejo Mini Park
places.summary: A 0.11-acre mini park at Hyde and Vallejo Streets, on the Powell-Hyde cable car line. It is open 5 a.m. to midnight.
places.history: No source states a description or a history for it.

places.name: Washington & Hyde Mini Park
places.summary: A 0.16-acre mini park at Washington and Hyde Streets. Its playground is built as a colourful child-size city with soft rubber flooring.
places.history: No source states when the playground was built.

places.name: Cheese Plus
places.summary: A cheese shop at Polk Street and Pacific Avenue, selling cheese, charcuterie, specialty foods, sandwiches, salads and wine. Open Monday to Friday 10 a.m. to 7.30 p.m., Saturday 9 a.m. to 7.30 p.m. and Sunday 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. Telephone (415) 921-2001.
places.history: No source states a history for the business.

places.name: Russian Hill Bookstore
places.summary: A bookshop on Polk Street selling used and new books, note cards, gifts, children's toys and board games. Telephone (415) 929-0997.
places.history: No source outside the shop's own site states a history for it.

places.name: Frascati
places.summary: A restaurant at Hyde and Green Streets, on the block the Powell-Hyde cable car runs along. Telephone (415) 928-1406.
places.history: No source states a history for the restaurant.

places.name: Za Pizza
places.summary: A pizzeria at Hyde and Green Streets serving thin-crust pizza, salads, wine and beer. Open daily from noon to 8 p.m. Telephone (415) 771-3100.
places.history: No source states when the pizzeria opened.

entries.name: Lombard Street's crooked block
entries.note: Eight hairpin turns of red brick built in 1922 between Hyde and Leavenworth, one way downhill, with a sign at the top recommending 5 miles per hour.

entries.name: Macondray Lane
entries.note: A pedestrian lane between Leavenworth and Taylor with a view to Alcatraz, which Armistead Maupin named in 2017 as the model for Barbary Lane.

entries.name: Russian Hill-Vallejo Street Crest District
entries.note: The crest that escaped the 1906 fire, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1988, reference number 87002289, on grades of 16, 23 and 40 percent.

entries.name: San Francisco Art Institute
entries.note: Bakewell & Brown's 1926 campus, San Francisco Landmark No. 85, designated in 1977; the school closed in July 2022 and the campus sold in 2024.

entries.name: Feusier Octagon House
entries.note: An eight-sided house of about 1857, San Francisco Landmark No. 36, designated in 1970; one of three octagon houses in San Francisco, and privately occupied.

entries.name: Engine Company No. 31 Fire House
entries.note: A fire house of 1908 on Green Street, San Francisco Landmark No. 220, designated in 1998, and listed on the National Register in 1988, reference number 87002290.

entries.name: Alhambra Theater
entries.note: Miller & Pflueger's Moorish Revival cinema of 1926, with 1,625 seats and a domed ceiling, now a gym behind the restored marquee.

entries.name: Church for the Fellowship of All Peoples
entries.note: An intercultural, interracial and interfaith congregation on Larkin Street whose October Convocation is open to the public.

entries.name: Broadway Tunnel
entries.note: The Robert C. Levy Tunnel, 1,616 feet in two bores, opened on 21 December 1952 on a 5 million dollar bond that voters approved in 1948.

entries.name: Francisco Park
entries.note: Four and a half acres opened in April 2022 on the site of the 1859 Francisco Reservoir, open 5 a.m. to midnight, with a dog run and a community garden.

entries.name: Fay Park
entries.note: A terraced garden designed by Thomas Church in 1957 and open to the public since 2006, but only from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., so plan the day around it.

entries.name: Ina Coolbrith Park
entries.note: A steep 0.87-acre park at Vallejo and Taylor, named for the writer and librarian Ina Coolbrith, open 5 a.m. to midnight.

entries.name: Frascati
entries.note: A restaurant at Hyde and Green Streets, on the block the Powell-Hyde cable car runs along.

entries.name: Cheese Plus
entries.note: Cheese, charcuterie, sandwiches and wine at Polk Street and Pacific Avenue, open from 10 a.m. on weekdays and 9 a.m. at weekends.

links.note: The waterfront at the foot of the hill: Ghirardelli Square, the Haslett Warehouse, Aquatic Park and the Hyde Street Pier, where the Powell-Hyde cable car ends.
